title: The Fir-Tree and the Bramble
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Fir-tree was boasting to a Bramble, and said, somewhat contemptuously, "You poor creature, you are of no use whatever. Now, look at me: I am useful for all sorts of things, particularly when men build houses; they can't do without me then." But the Bramble replied, "Ah, that's all very well: but you wait till they come with axes and saws to cut you down, and then you'll wish you were a Bramble and not a Fir."
Better poverty without a care than wealth with its many obligations.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who is the Fir-tree boasting to?
options: A nearby Oak
A group of travellers
A Bramble
A flock of birds

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fir-tree call the Bramble?
options: A poor creature of no use whatever
A dangerous plant to be avoided
A rival not worth noticing
A useful friend to the forest

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fir-tree say it is useful for?
options: Shading travellers from the sun
Feeding animals with its needles
Marking the boundary of the forest
All sorts of things, particularly when men build houses

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fir-tree say men can't do without it?
options: Making fires
Building houses
Crossing rivers
Growing crops

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Bramble say will eventually come for the Fir-tree?
options: A storm strong enough to uproot it
Insects that will eat away its bark
Axes and saws to cut it down
A drought that will dry it out

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Bramble predict the Fir-tree will wish for?
options: That it were a Bramble and not a Fir
That it had grown somewhere safer
That it had never boasted at all
That it could be replanted elsewhere

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Bramble mention the axes and saws?
options: To warn the Fir-tree about a fire spreading nearby
To boast about its own usefulness in comparison
To ask the Fir-tree for help defending itself
To point out that the Fir-tree's very usefulness is what puts it in danger

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Bramble's safety from being cut down depend on?
options: Growing in a place no one can reach
Being seen as having little value worth harvesting
Being protected by nearby trees like the Fir
Having thorns that keep people away entirely

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "contemptuously" mean in "said, somewhat contemptuously"?
options: In a way that shows fear or worry
In a way that shows deep sadness
In a way that shows scorn or disrespect
In a way that shows confusion

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable, given its closing line?
options: Being valuable to others can come at the cost of one's own safety
Brambles are more useful than most people realize
Boasting always leads to a swift punishment
Trees that build houses are safer than those left in the wild

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what tone does the Fir-tree use when it speaks to the Bramble?
options: Warm and friendly
Nervous and uncertain
Playful and joking
Somewhat contemptuous

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Bramble respond to being called useless?
options: By agreeing entirely with the Fir-tree
By pointing out a future danger the Fir-tree will face
By asking the Fir-tree to apologize
By boasting about its own thorns

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what two tools does the Bramble mention?
options: Hammers and nails
Ropes and pulleys
Axes and saws
Shovels and rakes

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the Fir-tree's confidence be short-sighted?
options: It overlooks that being valued for a purpose means eventually being used up for it
It fails to notice that the Bramble is actually stronger than it appears
It assumes houses will never need repairs in the future
It ignores that other trees are just as useful as it is

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Bramble seem to value more than being praised for usefulness?
options: Being admired by other plants
Being useful to builders as well
Being taller than the Fir-tree
Being left alone and safe from harm

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "obligations" mean in the closing line "wealth with its many obligations"?
options: Rewards earned through hard work
Burdens or responsibilities that come with something
Debts owed to another person
Compliments given by others

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Fir-tree and a Bramble become close friends after their argument
A Bramble is cut down while the Fir-tree remains safe
A boastful Fir-tree is warned that its very usefulness will one day lead to its downfall
A Fir-tree apologizes for insulting the Bramble
